newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine analysts see slim hope for Alfonsin bid.
newsitem.headline: Argentine analysts see slim hope for Alfonsin bid.

text.p: Former Argentine President Raul Alfonsin staged an impressive comeback into the limelight with a 20,000-strong rally on Wednesday, but analysts say he is unlikely to succeed in a new bid for the presidency.
"He cannot get more than 10 or 12 percent of the votes for president. He has a very slim chance of being candidate," said leading Argentine pollster Manuel Mora y Araujo.

Political analyst Rosendo Fraga agreed. The Radical Party politico who ruled Argentina between 1983-1989 "is in a very poor position as a candidate," he said. "For president ... he would barely manage three percent."

The 69-year-old Alfonsin, who came to power in 1983 after seven years of a brutal military dictatorship, relaunched his political career on Wednesday with a speech celebrating his election victory 13 years ago. He bitterly attacked Peronist President Carlos Menem's free-market policies, accusing him of being a puppet whose strings were pulled by the White House.

"These days the big decisions in Argentina are made in Washington and in international financial centres," Alfonsin told roaring fans at a rally. He urged Argentines to fight to remain a "nation" rather than become a "colony."

But even the centre-left Frepaso senator, Graciela Fernandez Meijide, considered the speech "too seventies and antiquated." While people enjoyed the nostalgia of the speech, "it does not mean they will vote for him," she said.

Despite his denials, the rally was widely interpreted as Alfonsin's first step in a campaign to win the Radical Party's nomination to run in 1999's presidential election. He said last week he would seek the nomination, "but if in 1998 I see my candidacy is not useful to the country, to democracy, then I will step down from the 1999 race."
Analyst Hugo Haime said Alfonsin was still viewed as the man "who oversaw the return of democracy after dictatorship. But apart from that, his image is very negative."

Alfonsin was elected president with 52 percent of the vote in 1983 after seven years' of the military's "Dirty War" in which tens of thousands of Argentines "disappeared" into clandestine torture centres and anonymous mass graves.
Alfonsin took the military junta chiefs to court where they were sentenced to life in jail. But Menem pardoned them right after he came to power in 1989.

Alfonsin's success in human rights was overshadowed by dismal management of the economy, which by the end of his mandate was in chaos with inflation running at 200 percent a month, supermarkets being looted and constant labour strikes.
His return to politics was welcomed by the ruling Peronists. "In the Radical Party he is one of the men with the highest prestige. He has incredible strength," said Menem.
But some analysts cynically suggested the Peronists are exhultant about Alfonsin's latest bid for power because they too are convinced his chances of success are virtually nil.
